Newsom made the comments while conducting a public outreach effort to address the all-but-certain recall.{{cite web|url=https://politi.co/2Qf1Pgg|title=Newsom's 'Zoom school' experience was in the past, office confirms|first=Mackenzie|last=Mays|website=[[Politico|Politico Pro]]|date=March 19, 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://politi.co/38AJCQK|title=Newsom relied on Dodgers, donor-driven foundation for splashy state speech|first=Jeremy B.|last=White|website=[[Politico|Politico Pro]]|date=March 12, 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250067849.html|title=Fact check: Are Gavin Newsom's kids 'living through Zoom school'?|website=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|first=Lara|last=Korte}} The [[COVID-19 pandemic in California]] led to widespread school closures, the emergence of distance learning, and student mental health and academic challenges, and by the summer of 2021, education became a prominent issue in the recall campaign. Republican candidates said the public K–12 school system failed to adequately serve students after teachers unions' demands led to extended shutdowns, and proposed a statewide voucher system, whereby parents could use their share of per-pupil state funding on the public, charter, or private school of their [[school choice|choice]].{{cite news|url=https://calmatters.org/education/2021/07/newsom-recall-candidates-education/|title=Newsom recall: GOP challengers see parents as 'consumers'|first=Joe|last=Hong|date=July 28, 2021|website=CalMatters}} Ahead of the September recall election, President [[Joe Biden]] and Vice President [[Kamala Harris]] campaigned for Newsom.{{cite web|url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/Kamala-Harris-says-she-will-campaign-for-Gavin-16329726.php|title=Kamala Harris says she will campaign for Gavin Newsom in recall fight|date=July 21, 2021|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]|first=Tal|last=Kopan}}{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/08/12/biden-comes-to-newsoms-recall-defense-as-white-house-mulls-larger-role-1389876|website=[[Politico]]|title=Biden comes to Newsom's recall defense as White House mulls larger role|first=Jeremy B.|last=White|date=August 12, 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article253768158.html|website=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|title=Kamala Harris to miss Gavin Newsom's recall defense rally after deadly Kabul bombings|first1=Sophia|last1=Bollag|first2=Lara|last2=Karte}}{{cite news |author=Faith E. Pinho |author2=Seema Mehta |author3=Julia Wick |author4=Robin Estrin |url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-13/biden-newsom-elder-campaign-california-recall|title=In final campaign push with Newsom, Biden says 'eyes of the nation' are on California recall|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|date=September 13, 2021}}{{cite news |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/biden-campaign-with-california-governor-eve-republican-backed-recall-election-2021-09-13/|work=Reuters|title=Biden campaigns with California governor on eve of Republican-backed recall election|first= Steve |last=Holland|date=September 14, 2021}} At a rally in [[Long Beach, California|Long Beach]] on the eve of the election, Biden said, "Folks, send a message to the nation: courage matters, leadership matters, science matters. Vote to keep Gavin Newsom." Both Biden and Newsom likened the frontrunner candidate Larry Elder to Trump, with Newsom warning, "We may have defeated Donald Trump, but we have not defeated [[Trumpism]]. Trumpism is still on the ballot in California." Newsom's campaign ran television ads in September 2021 that called his Republican opponents' positions "[[Anti-vaccine activism|anti-vax]]" and called the outcome of the recall vote "a matter of life and death."{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/business-health-coronavirus-pandemic-b6049fa972077f6baa2d0c9d3278debd|website=[[Associated Press]]|title=Gov. Newsom calls GOP rivals 'anti-vax,' but are they?|first1=Kathleen|last1=Ronayne|first2=Michael R.|last2=Blood|date=September 3, 2021}} All four major Republican candidates (Elder, Faulconer, Kiley, and Cox) opposed [[vaccine mandate]]s, although none contended that the vaccines were dangerous and all said that they had been [[COVID-19 vaccine|vaccinated against the virus]]. Among the Republican candidates, Faulconer was the strongest advocate of COVID-19 vaccination; Cox had an "evolving position" but eventually recommended that everyone get vaccinated against COVID-19, and Elder and Kiley said that individuals should make up their own minds. Elder pledged, if elected, to repeal all face-covering and COVID-19 testing requirements for state workers. ==== Newsom under recall ==== Although the recall petition was introduced in February 2020, before the onset of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], Newsom's response faced scrutiny by recall supporters and the news media.{{cite news|title=Why do people want to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom? We explain|date=February 2, 2021|url=https://abc7news.com/recall-newsom-petition-gov-update-status-signature-count/10256979/|first= Alix| last=Martichoux|publisher=[[KGO-TV]]}} Many in favor of recalling Newsom cited issues unrelated to the pandemic as reasons for their support.{{cite news|title=Did Gavin Newsom do anything wrong? It wasn't just the French Laundry that led to the recall|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article252824993.html|date=August 1, 2021| first= Sophia| last= Bollag| publisher= [[Sacramento Bee]]}} Newsom presided over an unexpected surplus in the state's 2021 finances, attributable to the recovery in the stock market, [[State income tax#California|the state's progressive tax code]], and [[American Rescue Plan Act of 2021|$26 billion in federal aid]], and announced a $100 billion post-pandemic spending proposal in May 2021 which would expand the eligibility for stimulus checks issued by the state to higher-wage earners with an additional payment to those with children, provide rental and utility assistance, and give funds to small businesses.{{cite web|url=https://www.abc10.com/article/news/local/california/calmatters/newsoms-spending-proposal/103-4b7c3418-2873-43f2-a465-bb044984e377|title=3 things to know about Gov. Newsom's spending proposal|website=[[KXTV]]|first=Laurel|last=Rosenhall|date=May 14, 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-05-15/federal-stimulus-politics-governors|last1=Mason|first1=Melanie|title=Gusher of federal stimulus funds a gift for governors like Gavin Newsom|date=May 15, 2021|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]}} While Newsom was required to return some of the surplus to taxpayers due to the [[Paul Gann|Gann limit]], which requires surplus funds to "be returned by a revision of tax rates or fee schedules", the [[Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association]] said the law was likely being misapplied with the issuance of rebate checks to targeted constituencies rather than with the reduction of tax rates for all taxpayers.{{cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/patrickgleason/2021/07/30/blue-state-taxpayers-to-receive-a-reprieve/|website=[[Forbes]]|title=Blue State Taxpayers To Receive A Reprieve|first=Patrick|last=Gleason|date=July 30, 2021}} A report from the nonpartisan [[Legislative Analyst's Office]], published shortly after the proposal was revealed, said that when considering spending that must go towards public schools, pay off debt, or be placed in the state's main reserve account, the surplus was actually $38 billion, not $75 billion as claimed by Newsom, that the proposal was being rushed since more time was needed to determine which solutions would be effective, and that the proposal was "shortsighted and inadvisable" since it requested $12 billion from the state's existing reserves in spite of the surplus.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-05-20/skelton-legislative-analysts-report-on-newsom-spending-borrowing-surplus|title=Column: Newsom is admonished for his big-spending budget by Sacramento's legislative analyst|first=George|last=Skelton|date=May 20, 2021|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-05-17/newsom-budget-relies-on-reserve-funds-analyst-report|title=Even with huge California surplus, Newsom's budget relies on reserves, analyst says|first=John|last=Myers|date=May 17, 2021|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}{{cite web|url=https://fox40.com/news/california-connection/analyst-criticizes-newsoms-spending-plan-as-shortsighted/|title=Analyst criticizes Newsom's spending plan as 'shortsighted'|date=May 18, 2021|agency=[[Associated Press]]|website=[[KTXL]]|access-date=May 18, 2021|archive-date=May 18, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518044204/https://fox40.com/news/california-connection/analyst-criticizes-newsoms-spending-plan-as-shortsighted/|url-status=dead}} Newsom's Democratic predecessor [[Jerry Brown]] said the spending plans were "not sustainable" and said, "I would predict, certainly within two years, we're going to see fiscal stress."{{cite news|url=https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/07/newsom-budget-jerry-brown/|website=CalMatters|title='Not sustainable': Jerry Brown bursts Newsom's budget bubble|first=Emily|last=Hoeven|date=July 14, 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://sjvsun.com/news/politics/carecall/newsoms-recall-spending-spree-prompts-a-word-of-warning-from-jerry-brown/|title=Newsom's recall spending spree prompts a word of warning – from Jerry Brown|first=Alex|last=Tavlian|date=July 12, 2021|website=The Sun}} Proponents of Newsom's proposal said the high amount of spending was "historic" and would help the economy recover from the pandemic, while opponents said Newsom's proposal was crafted in response to the imminent recall election.{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2021/05/10/995624284/facing-a-recall-and-a-massive-surplus-gov-newsom-proposes-more-stimulus-checks|title=Facing A Recall And A Massive Surplus, Gov. Newsom Proposes More Stimulus Checks|website=[[NPR]]|date=May 10, 2021|first=Nicole|last=Nixon}} According to state officials, a stimulus payment would be issued to eligible individuals starting in September 2021.{{cite web|url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/New-round-of-California-stimulus-checks-approved-16288273.php|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]|title=Here's when California's new round of $600 of stimulus checks are coming|first=Jessica|last=Flores|date=July 1, 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://www.abc10.com/article/news/verify/verify-relief-package-newsom/103-28b9f644-9df6-446f-ba64-ca804e0c72d5|website=[[KXTV]]|title=No, the relief package signed by Governor Newsom will not provide 'immediate' relief|first=Lena|last=Howland|date=July 13, 2021}} The first round of 600,000 stimulus checks was directly deposited into bank accounts on August 27, 2021, with payments to other recipients scheduled to be disbursed every two weeks.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-31/state-stimulus-checks-arrive-as-california-voters-cast-ballots-recall-election|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|title=State stimulus checks arrive in Californians' bank accounts ahead of recall election|first=Patrick |last=McGreevy|date=August 31, 2021|access-date=August 31, 2021}} In May 2021, ''[[Kaiser Health News]]'' reported that throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, Newsom was "routinely outsourcing life-or-death public health duties to his allies in the private sector" with lucrative no-bid government contracts. The report said the "vast majority" of awardees were Newsom supporters and donors who had collectively donated $113 million to his political campaigns (including to his campaign to fight the recall), charitable causes, or policy initiatives, since his entry into state-level politics in 2010.{{cite web|url=https://khn.org/news/article/how-newsoms-reliance-on-big-tech-in-pandemic-undermines-public-health-system/|title=Salesforce, Google, Facebook. How Big Tech Undermines California's Public Health System.|first=Angela|last=Hart|date=May 6, 2021|website=KHN.org}} In June 2021, ''[[The Sacramento Bee]]'' reported that the non-profit organization founded by Newsom's wife, [[Jennifer Siebel Newsom]], had received over $800,000 in donations from companies that lobbied or did business with California state government, and paid her over $2.3 million since 2011 for leading the organization and producing documentary films through her production company, Girl's Club Entertainment. When questioned about his wife's non-profit, Newsom denied that there was any conflict of interest with the arrangement.{{cite web|title=Gavin Newsom Says Corporate Donations to His Wife's Nonprofit Caused No Conflict of Interest|url=https://www.newsweek.com/gavin-newsom-says-corporate-donations-his-wifes-nonprofit-caused-no-conflict-interest-1597850|website=[[Newsweek]]|last=Pedroja|first=Cammy|date=June 4, 2021|access-date=July 2, 2021}} In response to the report, several recall challengers called for a ban on donations to non-profit organizations of elected officials' family members from companies engaged in business with the state.{{cite web|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article252170748.html|title=Curb nonprofit donations? Republicans running in Newsom recall say it would reduce conflicts|website=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|last=Bollag|first=Sophia|date=June 18, 2021|access-date=July 2, 2021}} ==== Partisanship ==== The recall effort was not launched by the state Republican Party apparatus, but rather by activists who had unsuccessfully attempted to recall Newsom before; the activists said the party establishment did not get involved in a substantial way until the recall effort had almost triggered the election.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-09-16/california-republican-future-after-recall|title=After recall flop, struggling California Republicans once again fighting over future|website=The Los Angeles Times|last1=Mason|first1=Melanie|last2=Mehta|first2=Seema|date=September 16, 2021}} Newsom did not acknowledge the recall election until its occurrence became all but certain, calling the effort "partisan, Republican". He recruited nationwide Democrats to help fundraise against it.{{cite web|url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/newsom-blames-extremists-for-recall|title=California's Newsom blames 'anti-mask and anti-vax extremists' for recall effort, vows to fight|work=[[Fox News]]|date=March 15, 2021|access-date=March 15, 2021|archive-date=March 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210315192300/https://www.foxnews.com/politics/newsom-blames-extremists-for-recall|url-status=live|first=Houston|last=Keene}}{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/03/15/warren-sanders-join-newsom-to-fight-extremist-gop-recall-1368279|title=Warren, Sanders join Newsom to fight 'extremist' GOP recall|first=Carla|last=Marinucci|work=[[Politico]]|date=March 15, 2021|access-date=March 15, 2021|archive-date=March 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210315192329/https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/03/15/warren-sanders-join-newsom-to-fight-extremist-gop-recall-1368279|url-status=live}} State Democratic leaders warned members of their party against running in the recall election to avoid a potential split electorate, which some attribute to the [[2003 California gubernatorial recall election|2003 recall]] of Governor [[Gray Davis]], where Democratic lieutenant governor [[Cruz Bustamante]] was defeated in his candidacy by Republican [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]].{{cite web |last1=White |first1=Jeremy B. |last2=Marinucci |first2=Carla |last3=Yamamura |first3=Kevin |title=Newsom swats away Democratic challengers. Will his party live to regret it? |url=https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/03/24/newsom-swats-away-democratic-challengers-will-his-party-live-to-regret-it-1369438 |website=[[Politico|Politico Pro]] |access-date=April 14, 2021 |language=en |date=March 24, 2021|archive-date=March 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210326210746/https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/03/24/newsom-swats-away-democratic-challengers-will-his-party-live-to-regret-it-1369438|url-status=live}} A May 2021 [[UC Berkeley]] Institute of Government Studies poll sponsored by the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' found that Democratic voters overwhelmingly preferred having a prominent Democratic replacement candidate on the ballot in case the recall was successful, at odds with attempts by party leadership to prevent such a scenario.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-05-11/opposition-grows-gavin-newsom-recall-poll|title=Opposition to Newsom recall grows as Caitlyn Jenner, GOP generate little support, poll finds|first=Phil|last=Willon|date=May 11, 2021|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]}} Former Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger disputed the supposed partisan motives of the recall, comparing the 2021 effort to the successful 2003 recall and saying,
It's pretty much the same atmosphere today as it was then. There was dissatisfaction, to the highest level. And it's the same with the momentum. Something that sets it off to a higher level, kind of the straw that breaks the camel's back{{nbsp}}... like an explosion.{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2021/03/31/arnold-schwarzenegger-newsom-california-recall-478575|work=[[Politico]]|date=March 31, 2021|title=Arnold Schwarzenegger has a warning for Gavin Newsom|first=Carla|last=Marinucci}}
Democratic strategist Katie Merrill said that the chance for a successful recall in 2021 was low:
Politically, we're a completely different state than we were in 2003. If you look at the statewide races, the Republican Party has effectively become a third party in California.{{cite news|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/different-time-why-recall-effort-against-california-gov-newsom-not-n1263392|first=Alicia Victoria|last=Lozano|title='A Different Time': Why the Recall Effort Against California Gov. Newsom Isn't History Repeating|date=April 7, 2021|work=[[NBC News]]|access-date=April 23, 2021}}
Newsom sought to connect the backers of the recall effort to "the RNC, anti-mask and anti-vax extremists, and pro-Trump forces", while recall proponents said that the recall was only about Newsom and his performance as governor, and claimed that around one third of recall petition signatories were registered Democrats or independents.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-03-16/gavin-newsom-recall-election-trump-covid-19-campaigns-republicans-democrats|title=Gavin Newsom and Democrats are dragging Donald Trump into the recall fight|author=Phil Willon|date=March 16, 2021|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]}} By April{{nbsp}}30, 2021, nearly a year after the recall campaign was approved for petition circulation by the secretary of state, Trump had yet to personally comment on the recall effort.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/newsletter/2021-03-15/making-california-recall-newsom-about-trump-essential-politics|title=Essential Politics: Making California's recall about Trump|date=March 15, 2021|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|first=John|last=Myers}} In September 2021, Trump commented on the recall election, claiming without evidence that it was "probably rigged".{{cite web|url=https://www.sfgate.com/gavin-newsom-recall/Trump-recall-voter-fraud-rigged-Newsom-ballot-mail-16442942.php|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle|SFGate]]|title=Trump, without evidence, already claiming Gavin Newsom recall election is 'rigged'|first=Eric|last=Ting|date=September 8, 2021|access-date=September 8, 2021}} Despite the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|CDC]]'s mid-May guidance that it was not necessary for persons fully vaccinated against COVID-19 to wear masks in most indoor settings, Newsom's administration decided that California would continue its indoor mask mandate for another month, until June 15, 2021. Reception to the CDC's new guidance among public health experts had been mixed, with some favoring quick implementation and others favoring a delay, including Bob Wachter, chair of the UCSF Department of Medicine, who called the CDC's new guidance "premature".{{cite web|url=https://www.kqed.org/news/11874066/when-can-you-stop-wearing-a-mask-in-california-state-says-june-15-2|title=When Can You Stop Wearing a Mask in California? State Says June 15|website=[[KQED Inc.|KQED]]|first=Matthew|last=Green|date=May 17, 2021}} The delayed implementation was criticized by [[UCSF]] scientist and COVID-19 expert Dr. [[Monica Gandhi]] who said it had no scientific rationale, while potentially causing harm by suggesting there is "still a danger when there isn't one".{{cite web|url=https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/2021-05-California-mask-mandate-CDC-vaccinated-new-16177861.php|title=UCSF expert: California, San Francisco should 'immediately' lift mask mandates for vaccinated|date=May 14, 2021|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle|SFGate]]|first=Eric|last=Ting}} Isaac Hale, a lecturer of political science at [[UC Davis]], said partisan politics concerning the recall may have been a factor in the decision:
One of [the] top political priorities Newsom has is keeping the Democratic base together, which is why they're really focused on arguing the recall is a partisan Republican endeavor. The biggest thing that could damage that narrative is if a prominent Democrat or progressive emerged as a candidate in the recall, like [[Cruz Bustamante]] did in 2003. The key to Newsom staying in power is keeping the Democratic base happy, consolidated and making sure the California Democratic Party is the party of Gavin Newsom, and Gavin Newsom only. It's smart politics since mask mandates are popular among California Democrats.{{cite web|url=https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Gavin-Newsom-recall-mask-mandate-CDC-June-15-COVID-16183415.php|title=How heavily did recall politics weigh on Gavin Newsom's mask decision?|date=May 17, 2021|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle|SFGate]]|first=Eric|last=Ting}}
[[Jack Citrin]], a political science professor at [[UC Berkeley]], said [[#Recall election timeline (SB 117 and SB 152)|changing the electoral calendar]] threatened to reinforce the public's cynicism about politicians using any means available to stay in power, and that they were "trying to create a situation that is most favorable for the partisan outcome that they favor".{{cite web|url=https://sanfrancisco.cbslocal.com/2021/06/27/newsom-recall-democrats-again-seek-to-alter-californias-recall-laws/?amp|title=Newsom Recall: Democrats Again Seeking To Alter California's Recall Laws|website=[[KPIX-TV]]|date=June 27, 2021|access-date=July 2, 2021}} The changes were heavily criticized by Newsom's Republican opponents.{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2021/07/01/1012338448/california-sets-sept-14-as-the-date-for-the-recall-election-targeting-gov-newsom|title=New, Earlier Date Puts GOP At A Disadvantage In California Recall Election|website=[[NPR]]|first=Nicole|last=Nixon|date=July 2, 2021}} In August, recall proponents filed suit challenging language proposed by Newsom for the voter information handbook, alleging it falsely or misleading characterized the recall as a "power grab" by "Republicans and Trump supporters".{{cite news|url=https://ktla.com/news/california/newsom-cant-tie-recall-election-to-gop-in-voter-guide-lawsuit-says/|title=Newsom can't tie recall election to GOP in voter guide, lawsuit says|agency=Associated Press|date=August 2, 2021|website=[[KTLA]]|archive-date=October 13, 2023|access-date=August 8, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231013170127/https://ktla.com/news/california/newsom-cant-tie-recall-election-to-gop-in-voter-guide-lawsuit-says/|url-status=dead}} On August{{nbsp}}5, 2021, Sacramento County Superior Court Judge Laurie{{nbsp}}M. Earl ruled against the suit and allowed inclusion of the disputed language, saying, "There is nothing false or misleading about describing the recall effort's leaders as Trump supporters."{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-05/court-ruling-final-newsom-may-blame-recall-on-republicans-and-trump-supporters/|title=Court ruling is final: Newsom may blame recall on 'Republicans and Trump supporters'|first=Maura|last=Dolan|date=August 5, 2021|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]}} Judge Earl wrote that while it may have been an exaggeration to describe the election as a "Republican recall", the rhetoric was "common to political debate" and "permissible".{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/08/04/newsom-can-reference-trump-in-argument-against-recall-judge-says-1389479|title=Newsom can reference Trump in argument against recall, judge says|first=Jeremy B.|last=White|date=August 4, 2021|website=[[Politico]]}} On July{{nbsp}}24, 2021, the California Republican Party's steering committee voted to allow the party to endorse a candidate in the recall election, if the candidate received at least 60{{nbsp}}percent of delegate votes in an upcoming August{{nbsp}}7 meeting. Some Republicans opposed the move out of concern that endorsing a single candidate would reduce Republican voter turnout.{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/07/24/california-republican-party-creates-recall-endorsement-path-1388974|title=California Republican Party creates recall endorsement path|first=Jeremy B.|last=White|date=July 24, 2021|website=[[Politico]]}} On August{{nbsp}}7, the party voted to cancel the endorsement vote and issue no endorsement;{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/08/07/california-gop-wont-endorse-a-candidate-in-newsom-recall-1389718|title=California GOP won't endorse a candidate in Newsom recall|first=Jeremy B.|last=White|date=August 7, 2021|website=[[Politico]]}} prior to the cancellation of the endorsement vote, Republican delegates were set to choose an endorsee from the four candidates who each had received the support of at least 200 delegates, which were [[Larry Elder]], [[Kevin Faulconer]], [[Kevin Kiley (politician)|Kevin Kiley]], and [[Doug Ose]].{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-07/cagop-endorsement-vote-jenner-elder-faulconer-ose-kiley|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|title=State GOP votes not to endorse a candidate in the recall race|first=Seema|last=Mehta|date=August 7, 2021}} With political allies having successfully dissuaded prospective high-level Democrats from joining the race, Newsom's campaign urged supporters to skip the second question on the recall ballot. The directive was criticized by nonpartisan political observers, who said that it was misleading and could cause voter confusion.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-09/newsom-wants-voters-to-skip-the-recall-ballots-second-part-they-dont-have-to|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|title=Newsom wants voters to ignore the recall ballot's second question. They don't have to|first1=John|last1=Myers|first2=Seema|last2=Mehta|date=August 9, 2021}} === Recall election (September 2021) === ==== Election administration ==== After some blueprints of the [[Dominion Voting Systems]] voting machines were leaked, a group of eight cybersecurity experts called, in a letter to Secretary of State [[Shirley Weber]], for rigorous auditing of the recall election with a [[risk-limiting audit]] to mitigate any cyberattack risk. The experts wrote that they had no evidence of a hacking threat, and did not cast any blame on Dominion, but said that the state and counties should take steps to ensure that "the release of the Dominion software into the wild" did not increase election security risks.{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/technology-california-4e0e59da8bd5618c653b3e3fab524d2e|website=[[Associated Press]]|title=Experts call for rigorous audit to protect California recall|first1=Christina A.|last1=Cassidy|first2=Kate|last2=Brumback|date=September 3, 2021|access-date=September 3, 2021}} The California Secretary of State's office said the 40 counties in California using Dominion election management system use a different version of the software that meets state requirements, and noted that California election systems have layered security protections, including routine vulnerability testing, pre-election testing, access controls, and physical security. California also uses paper ballots with a [[voter-verified paper audit trail]], another security measure. ==== Larry Elder's unsubstantiated fraud claim prior to election day ==== The day before the end of voting, candidate Larry Elder claimed on his campaign website that fraud had already been detected and linked to a petition for citizens to sign "demanding a special session of the California legislature to investigate and ameliorate the twisted results" of the election,{{cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/newsom-leads-california-recall-polls-larry-elder-pushes-baseless-fraud-n1279080|title=As Newsom leads California recall polls, Larry Elder pushes baseless fraud claims|website=[[NBC News]]|first=Alex|last=Seitz-Wald|date=September 13, 2021|access-date=September 13, 2021}} though no vote totals had yet been reported. The post also referred to Newsom having been "reinstated," leading NBC news to speculate that the post had been intended for publication the following day and mistakenly released early, and that the Elder campaign had anticipated that Elder would lose. Elder would concede defeat on election day. His claim that cast doubt on the legitimacy of the election result was accompanied by similar unsubstantiated claims from former president [[Donald Trump]] and several right-wing media figures.{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/09/10/politics/fact-check-republican-claims-recall-rigged-stolen/index.html|title=Republicans are laying the groundwork to lie that the California recall was stolen|first=Daniel |last=Dale |website=CNN}} == California's recall process == {{See also|1911 California Proposition 8}} [[File:2021_California_Gubernatorial_recall_election_ballot_--_Los_Angeles_County.jpg|thumb|right|An image of a [[ballot]] from [[Los Angeles County]]. The listed order of the replacement candidates was determined by a randomization of the alphabet. The starting point, however, gets shifted for each of the [[California State Assembly Districts|state's 80 Assembly Districts]] (hence, all 46 candidates appear at the top of the ballot in at least one assembly district, with 34 candidates being listed first in two assembly districts).{{cite web|url=https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/randomized-alphabet|title=Randomized Alphabet :: California Secretary of State|publisher=[[California Secretary of State]]}}]] As of 2021, California is one of 19 states to allow recall elections.{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/elections-coronavirus-pandemic-california-arnold-schwarzenegger-gavin-newsom-87f78b119844ffc309549fdd0d07078f|title=Recall of State Officials|last=Blood|first=Michael R.|date=March 17, 2021|website=[[Associated Press]]|access-date=April 6, 2021|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210406050459/https://apnews.com/article/elections-coronavirus-pandemic-california-arnold-schwarzenegger-gavin-newsom-87f78b119844ffc309549fdd0d07078f|archive-date=April 6, 2021}} Under state law, any elected official may be subjected to a recall.{{Cite constitution|article=II|section=13|polity=California|date=June 8, 1976|url=https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2015.&article=II}} To trigger a recall election of a statewide elected official, proponents must gather a certain number of signatures from registered voters within a certain time period. The number must equal at least 12 percent of the votes cast in the previous election for that office.{{Cite constitution|article=II|clause=B|section=14|polity=California|date=June 8, 1976|url=https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2015.&article=II}}{{cite web|url=https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/politics/newsom-recall-reaches-60-percent-of-goal-over-holiday-with-two-months-to-deadline|title=Newsom recall reaches 60 percent of goal over holiday with two months to deadline|last=Blankley|first=Bethany|date=January 5, 2021|website=[[Washington Examiner]]|access-date=January 25, 2021|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210203074325/https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/politics/newsom-recall-reaches-60-percent-of-goal-over-holiday-with-two-months-to-deadline|archive-date=February 3, 2021}} Based on the [[2018 California gubernatorial election|previous gubernatorial election]], the 2021 recall petition required 1,495,709 signatures. When the [[Secretary of State of California|secretary of state]] confirms that a recall petition meets the required number of signatures, a recall election must be scheduled within 60 to 80 days.{{Cite constitution|article=II|clause=A|section=15|polity=California|date=November 8, 1994}}{{cite web|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/543955-whats-next-in-the-california-recall|title=What's next in the California recall|last=Wilson|first=Reid|date=March 19, 2021|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|access-date=March 19, 2021|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210319221549/https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/543955-whats-next-in-the-california-recall|archive-date=March 19, 2021}} If the petition qualifies fewer than 180 days prior to the next regularly scheduled election, then the recall becomes part of that regularly scheduled election.{{Cite constitution|article=II|clause=B|section=15|polity=California|date=November 8, 1994}} In the case of a recall against the governor, the responsibility for scheduling the recall election falls on the [[Lieutenant Governor of California|lieutenant governor]],{{cite web|url=https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf|title=Procedures for Recalling State and Local Officials|date=January 2020|publisher=[[California Secretary of State]]|access-date=February 1, 2021|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210203074426/https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf|archive-date=February 3, 2021}} which in 2021 was [[Eleni Kounalakis]]. A recall ballot in California consists of two parts: whether the incumbent should be recalled, and a selection of replacement candidates in the event they are recalled. If a simple [[majority]] of those who cast ballots favors removing the incumbent by selecting "YES" on the first question,{{cite web|url=https://abc7.com/gavin-newsom-recall-ballot-election-candidates/10904560/|title=Newsom recall effort: California's ballot could confuse voters. Here's what you need to know|website=[[KABC-TV]]|first=Josh|last=Haskell|date=July 22, 2021}} then the replacement candidate [[First-past-the-post voting|who receives the most votes]] (a type of [[plurality voting]]) finishes out the incumbent's term in office. A voter is allowed a single unranked vote when choosing a preferred replacement candidate, irrespective of their response to the first question.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/03/us/newsom-california-recall-ballot.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20211228/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/03/us/newsom-california-recall-ballot.html |archive-date=2021-12-28 |url-access=limited|website=[[The New York Times]]|title=Why Newsom Is Telling California Voters to Leave Half the Ballot Blank|first=Soumya|last=Karlamangla|date=September 3, 2021}}{{cbignore}} If the recall had been successful, the new governor would have taken office 38 days after the election and served the remainder of the term through January 2, 2023.{{cite web |title=California Gubernatorial Recall Election – Frequently Asked Questions |url=https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/2021-ca-gov-recall/newsom-recall-faqs |website=[[California Secretary of State]] |access-date=September 11, 2021 |archive-date=September 10, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210910124136/https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/2021-ca-gov-recall/newsom-recall-faqs }} Following legislation, all registered voters would be mailed a ballot for any elections held in 2021, including the recall election (subsequent legislation signed by Governor Newsom in September 2021 would mandate the same universal mail-in format for all future state and local elections).{{Cite web|url=https://www.kqed.org/news/11890023/california-adopts-vote-by-mail-system-for-all-future-elections|title=California Adopts Vote-by-Mail System for All Future Elections|website=KQED|date=September 28, 2021 }} === Changes to state recall election laws === Though California's recall process remains fundamentally unchanged since its introduction in 1911, beginning in 2017 and up to the 2021 gubernatorial recall, California's Democratic-led government enacted legislation to change how recall elections are conducted. Several lawmakers and academics also proposed more substantial changes during the 2021 recall campaign that would later fail in the legislature and the courts; similar rule changes were proposed during California's [[2003 recall election]] campaign that targeted Democrat Gray Davis.{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-16/how-much-did-the-california-recall-cost-maybe-300-million|title=California recall price tag could hit $300 million. Some say it was a waste of money|date=September 16, 2021|website=Los Angeles Times}} In addition, a new election law was applied to the 2021 recall election, though its application would later be ruled invalid in court. ==== Recall election timeline (SB 117 and SB 152) ==== In 2017, ahead of the successful recall of State Senator [[Josh Newman (politician)|Josh Newman]] (D-Fullerton), Democratic legislators changed the law concerning recall elections with Senate Bill 117{{cite web|url=https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180SB117|website=California Legislative Information|title=SB-117 Elections.|date=August 24, 2017}} to give voters 30 business days to withdraw their names from the recall petition.{{cite news|date=June 23, 2021| title=Newsom recall is a go after only 43 people remove their signatures from effort|url=https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/43-signatures-removed-california-governor-recall-petition/103-34d4f3e9-cca9-473b-8d09-74fce123a92b| first= Matthew| last= Nuttle|website=[[KXTV]]}} The 2017 law change also added a 30-day period for the state Department of Finance to conduct a cost estimate and gave the Joint Legislative Budget Committee 30 days to review the estimate.{{cite news|title=California Democrats again seek to alter recall laws|url=https://apnews.com/article/ca-state-wire-california-business-laws-government-and-politics-429db6821534040160dc65e49315836f|work=Associated Press|date=June 27, 2021|first= Kathleen| last= Ronayne}} On June 28, 2021, Newsom signed Senate Bill 152 into law, which allowed for his recall election to be held as early as August 2021 by allowing for a shorter recall timeline, which had been lengthened prior to the recall of Senator Newman.{{cite news|url=https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/06/lawmakers-accelerate-newsom-recall/|title=In switch, lawmakers accelerate Newsom recall election|first=Emily|last=Hoeven|date=June 11, 2021|website=CalMatters}} The changes allowed the lieutenant governor to set a date for the recall without waiting for the Joint Legislative Budget Committee to review the cost estimate "so long as the Legislature has appropriated the funds it determines 'reasonably necessary' to conduct the recall election".{{cite news|title=UPDATE: California Democrats change election rules ahead of Gavin Newsom recall|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article252420883.html|date=June 28, 2021|first =Lara| last= Korte|publisher=[[The Sacramento Bee]]}} With the same law change, the legislature appropriated $250 million to administer the recall election.{{cite news|title=New, Earlier Date Puts GOP At A Disadvantage In California Recall Election|url=https://www.npr.org/2021/07/01/1012338448/california-sets-sept-14-as-the-date-for-the-recall-election-targeting-gov-newsom|date= July 2, 2021| first=Nicole| last=Nixon|publisher=[[NPR]]}} ==== Election cost ==== While Newsom's pre-pandemic response to the recall effort in early 2020 warned that a special recall election would cost $81 million,{{Cite web|url=https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/recall-info/statement-answer.htm|title=Official Voter Information Guide | California Secretary of State|website=voterguide.sos.ca.gov}} county officials estimated in June 2021 that a statewide recall election, which at the time was expected to be held in the fall of 2021, would cost taxpayers $215 million.{{cite web|url=https://www.kron4.com/news/california/this-is-the-cost-for-the-california-recall-that-could-oust-newsom/|title=Cost for California recall that could oust Newsom: $215 million|website=[[KRON-TV]]|agency=[[Associated Press]]|date=June 10, 2020|access-date=September 17, 2021|archive-date=October 13, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231013165530/https://www.kron4.com/news/california/this-is-the-cost-for-the-california-recall-that-could-oust-newsom/|url-status=dead}} This higher estimate had presumed higher paper costs due to California's requirements for universal mail-in ballots instituted during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in California|COVID-19 pandemic]], which covered all elections held in 2020 and 2021, as well as a lengthy recall calendar featuring the rule changes enacted in 2017, ahead of Senator Newman's recall.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-06-17/elections-officials-alarmed-by-democrats-plans-change-newsom-recall-rules|title=Elections officials alarmed by Democrats' plans to change Newsom recall rules|first1=John|last1=Myers|date=June 17, 2021|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}{{cite web|url=https://ktla.com/news/california/dont-hold-newsom-recall-before-mid-september-california-county-clerks-urge/|title=Don't hold Newsom recall before mid-September, California county clerks urge|agency=[[Associated Press]]|website=[[KTLA]]|date=June 15, 2021|access-date=July 2, 2021|archive-date=June 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210616012917/https://ktla.com/news/california/dont-hold-newsom-recall-before-mid-september-california-county-clerks-urge/|url-status=dead}} With the shortened timeline from SB 152 now ensuring a summertime election, California's county election clerks nonetheless urged Lieutenant Governor Kounalakis to schedule the election as late as possible, citing an inability to guarantee a successful August election, possible voter confusion, and the potential for costs far beyond the original estimate. A summertime election, held in late August or early September, could have helped Newsom defeat the recall by avoiding political fallout over fires, virus variants, or school reopenings, which could coincide with what had been anticipated to be a late October or early November recall election; this strategic advantage was the rationale for public advocacy for an earlier election by Democratic state senator [[Steve Glazer]].{{cite web|url=https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Gavin-Newsom-recall-timeline-when-Republicans-date-16241523.php|title=Republicans rage after Dems move up Newsom recall timeline|first=Eric|last=Ting|date=June 11, 2021|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle|SFGate]]}} On July 1, the Department of Finance released an estimate of the cost of the September 14, 2021 election at $276 million, an increase of $61 million from the prior $215 million estimated by county election offices.{{cite news|title=California Recall: What To Know About The Effort To Remove Gavin Newsom|url=https://www.capradio.org/articles/2021/07/18/signatures-are-in-what-you-need-to-know-about-the-gavin-newsom-recall-effort/|date=July 18, 2021|first=Nicole|last=Nixon|website=[[KXJZ|Cap Radio]]}} Newsom's campaign and Democratic legislative leaders of both state houses had criticized the recall election as a waste of taxpayer money, while recall proponents said, "You can't put a price on democracy," and that some costs could have been avoided if officials allowed for a "traditional" election without universal mail-in ballots. While the projected $276 million cost of the recall was close to the $292 million spent on the [[2020 general election]] in California, which was the first to feature universal mail-in ballots, the cost per voter was significantly higher than in the [[2018 midterm elections]].{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/newsletter/2021-04-26/election-costs-gavin-newsom-recall-essential-politics|title=Essential Politics: A $400-million Newsom recall election?|date=April 26, 2021|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|first=John|last=Myers}} Secretary of State Weber said in an interview with ''[[KABC-TV]]'' that the recall election's total cost by election day had surpassed $276 million and was on track to eventually exceed $300 million.{{cite web|last=Sierra |first=Stephanie |url=https://abc7news.com/ca-recall-election-cost-of-gavin-newsom/11021178/ |title=California Recall: Election price tag 'could be' more than $300M, secretary of state says, as experts call for reform |website=[[KGO-TV]] |date=September 15, 2021 |access-date=September 15, 2021}} On February 3, 2022, election officials released a final tally of the costs for the recall election, at a little over $200.2 million.{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-02-03/california-recall-election-cost-200-million-dollars|title=California recall election cost $200 million, top elections official says|first1=John Myers John Myers leads the Los Angeles Times' coverage of state government as Sacramento bureau|last1=chief|first2=writes a weekly newsletter on California politics along with regular news|last2=analysis|date=February 4, 2022|website=Los Angeles Times}} ==== Incumbent's party preference (SB 151) ==== In 2019, Newsom signed Senate Bill 151 into law,{{cite web|url=https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200SB151|website=California Legislative Information|title=SB-151 Elections.|date=October 8, 2019}} which gave recall targets the right to state their party preference on the recall ballot. Newsom was unable to take advantage of the new law after his campaign missed a February 2020 deadline (when the recall petition was filed) to state his party preference. In June and July 2021, Newsom's campaign sued Secretary of State [[Shirley Weber]] (whom he appointed earlier in 2021) over the issue, but lost the case. Weber sided with him, telling the judge that voters would benefit from knowing Newsom's political party preference. The lawyers arguing the case in opposition to Newsom before Judge [[James P. Arguelles]] (who had also approved the recall signature deadline extension){{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/07/12/newsom-cant-label-himself-a-democrat-on-recall-ballot-1388231|title=Newsom can't label himself a Democrat on recall ballot|first=Jeremy B.|last=White|website=[[Politico|Politico Pro]]|date=July 12, 2021}} represented replacement candidate [[Caitlyn Jenner]] and proponents of the recall.{{cite web|url=https://www.capradio.org/167259|title=Gov. Newsom Sues Secretary Of State To Get Party Affiliation On Recall Ballot|first=Nicole|last=Nixon|website=[[KXJZ|Cap Radio]]|date=June 30, 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article252731678.html|title=Gavin Newsom loses court fight to be listed as a Democrat on recall ballot|website=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|first=Lara|last=Korte}} ==== Misapplication of tax return disclosure law (SB 27) ==== {{Main|California Senate Bill 27 (2019)|l1 = Senate Bill 27 (2019)}} A new requirement for gubernatorial candidates to disclose their most recent tax returns was passed into law in 2019, when Governor Newsom signed Senate Bill 27.{{notetag|The law also imposed a similar disclosure requirement on presidential candidates, primarily aimed at forcing [[Donald Trump]] to release his most recent tax returns [[2020 United States presidential election in California|when he ran in 2020]]. The disclosure requirement for presidential candidates was struck down by the courts.{{cite web|url=https://www.courthousenews.com/california-high-court-strikes-down-candidate-tax-return-law/|title=California High Court Strikes Down Candidate Tax Return Law|website=Court House News|last1=Cahill|first1=Nick|date=November 21, 2019|access-date=October 13, 2021}}}} Although the language of the law says that gubernatorial candidates must publicize the prior five years of their tax returns in order for their names to appear on a "primary ballot", the [[California Secretary of State|secretary of state]] applied the law to the recall election.{{cite news|title=Newsom releases tax return, but will recall candidates?|url=https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/gavin-newsom-taxes/| first= Laurel| last= Rosenhall|date=May 17, 2021|website=CalMatters}} The law has been cited as a potential reason for the major reduction in recall [[#Replacement candidates|replacement candidates]] relative to the number of candidates in the [[2003 California gubernatorial recall election|2003 gubernatorial recall]].{{cite news|url=https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/06/newsom-recall-tax-returns/|title=Will tax return rule scare off Newsom recall candidates?|website=CalMatters|last=Rosenhall|first=Laurel|date=June 30, 2021|access-date=July 2, 2021}} The tax return disclosure requirement did not apply to Newsom, who was not considered a "candidate" in the recall. Newsom's campaign nonetheless submitted his tax documents to Secretary of State [[Shirley Weber]], who refused to publish them on the grounds that the governor was not required to disclose them. Newsom's campaign did not respond to a reporter's July 19, 2021, request for his recent tax returns.{{cite web|url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2021/07/19/you-can-see-tax-returns-for-all-41-recall-candidates-but-not-gov-newsoms|title=You can see tax returns for all 41 recall candidates, but not Gov. Newsom's|date=July 19, 2021|first=Emily|last=Deruy|website=[[The Mercury News]]}} On July 21, 2021, [[Sacramento County Superior Court]] Judge Laurie Earl invalidated all tax return disclosure requirements for the 2021 recall election. The ruling was on a suit filed by prospective recall challenger [[Larry Elder]] against Secretary of State Weber, alleging she overstepped her authority by disqualifying him from his candidacy due to a purported tax return filing error.{{cite web|url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/Larry-Elder-added-to-California-recall-ballot-on-16330713.php|title=California recall ballot expands after judge tosses tax requirement|date=July 21, 2021|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]|first=Alexei|last=Koseff}} The judge ruled that Weber had improperly disqualified Elder, who had "substantially complied" with the requirements and that the special recall election was not a primary election and therefore Senate Bill 27 did not even apply.{{cite web|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article252932843.html|title=Recall ballot takes shape + Meet our new reporter + Garment workers push for better pay|website=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|first=Andrew|last=Sheeler|date=July 22, 2021}} By then, 42 candidates' tax returns had already been made public by the secretary of state's office.{{cite web|url=https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/07/newsom-recall-tax-returns-2/|title=Six things to know about the Newsom recall candidates' tax returns|date=July 20, 2021|website=CalMatters|first1=Laurel|last1=Rosenhall|first2=Sameea|last2=Kamal}} Weber's office said it would comply with the ruling and did not appeal.{{cite news|title=Judge puts Larry Elder on recall ballot, throws out tax return requirement| date= July 22, 2021| first= Laurel| last= Rosenhall |url=https://www.cbs8.com/article/news/local/california/calmatters/judge-larry-elder-recall-ballot-throws-out-tax-return-requirement/509-de2e869c-8516-465e-81fd-5cac0f7e9eaf|website=[[KFMB-TV]]}} ==== Constitutional legal challenge ==== In August 2021, an essay by [[UC Berkeley School of Law]] Dean [[Erwin Chemerinsky]] and UC Berkeley Professor of Law and Economics [[Aaron Edlin]] appeared in ''[[The New York Times]]'' claiming California's recall process violates the [[Constitution of the United States]], since more people could vote to retain Newsom than for any particular candidate while still ousting him, thus potentially violating "one person, one vote" legal precedent (conversely, if a majority of voters favored retaining Newsom, but an even greater number of voters favored a particular replacement candidate, Newsom would nonetheless prevail).{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/11/opinion/california-recall-election-newsom.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20211228/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/11/opinion/california-recall-election-newsom.html |archive-date=2021-12-28 |url-access=limited|website=[[The New York Times]]|title=There Is a Problem With California's Recall. It's Unconstitutional.|date=August 11, 2021|first1=Erwin|last1=Chemerinsky|first2=Aaron S.|last2=Edlin}}{{cbignore}}{{cite web|url=https://www.capradio.org/articles/2021/08/14/interview-legal-scholar-says-newsom-recall-is-unconstitutional/|website=[[KXJZ|Cap Radio]]|title=Interview: Legal Scholar Says Newsom Recall Is Unconstitutional|date=August 14, 2021|first1=Randol|last1=White}} [[Charles C. W. Cooke]], writing in ''[[The National Review]]'' in the same month, criticized the rationale and timing of the essay's publication and said Chemerinsky had selectively taken issue with California's recall, in which a Democrat was targeted, by not bringing up the pivotal [[2020–21 United States Senate election in Georgia]], which would also be invalid by his logic.{{cite web|url=https://www.nationalreview.com/2021/08/if-californias-recall-is-illegal-so-was-jon-ossoffs-election-in-georgia/|website=[[National Review]]|title=If California's Recall Is Illegal, So Was Jon Ossoff's Election in Georgia|date=August 12, 2021|first1=Charles C. W.|last1=Cooke}} Many experts have said the current recall process would probably survive legal challenges.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-22/newsom-could-be-replaced-by-recall-candidate-with-fewer-votes|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|title=California recall reality: Newsom could be replaced by candidate with far fewer votes|first=Maura|last=Dolan|date=August 22, 2021}} On August 13, 2021, two California voters filed a federal lawsuit against California's recall process, with formerly disbarred{{cite web|url=https://www.law.com/therecorder/2021/08/18/once-disbarred-civil-rights-attorney-now-fights-to-stop-the-newsom-recall/|website=[[ALM (company)|law.com]]|title=Once Disbarred, Civil Rights Attorney Now Fights to Stop the Newsom Recall|first=Cheryl|last=Miller|date=August 18, 2021}} attorney [[Stephen Yagman]] and Joseph Reichmann as counsel,{{cite web|url=https://www.sanluisobispo.com/news/california/article253546029.html|website=[[The Tribune (San Luis Obispo)|The Tribune]]|title=Is the California recall election unconstitutional? A new lawsuit makes the case|first1=Andrew|last1=Sheeler}} alleging violation of the U.S. Constitution's [[Equal Protection Clause]].{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/08/16/federal-lawsuit-challenges-california-recall-as-unconstitutional-1390127|website=[[Politico]]|title=Federal lawsuit challenges California recall as unconstitutional|date=August 16, 2021|first1=Jeremy B.|last1=White|first2=Debra|last2=Kahn}} [[California Attorney General]] [[Rob Bonta]] said on August 16, 2021, that he was monitoring the lawsuit and legal debate; by then, millions of ballots had already been sent out. On August 27, 2021, [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]] Judge [[Michael W. Fitzgerald]], an Obama appointee, dismissed the lawsuit.{{cite web|url=https://www.sfgate.com/gavin-newsom-recall/Lawsuit-recall-unconstitutional-Newsom-California-16417319.php|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle|SFGate]]|title=Lawsuit hoping to stop Gavin Newsom recall election fails|first=Eric|last=Ting|date=August 27, 2021}} Judge Fitzgerald, in his ruling, said of the plaintiffs' grievances: "Such disgruntlement raises no federal constitutional issues and certainly does not give the federal judiciary the right to halt the mammoth undertaking of this gubernatorial recall election."{{cite web|url=https://www.capradio.org/articles/2021/08/27/californias-recall-process-is-constitutional-federal-judge-rules/|website=[[KXJZ|Cap Radio]]|title=California's Recall Process Is Constitutional, Federal Judge Rules|first=Nicole|last=Nixon|date=August 27, 2021}} The office of [[California Secretary of State|Secretary of State]] [[Shirley Weber]] (the defendant in the case) said they would not appeal the ruling. ==== Proposed changes to state recall election law ==== In April 2021, two bills that could make future recalls less likely were introduced in the California Senate: the first, a bill originally authored by Senator [[Ben Allen (California politician)|Ben Allen]] (D-Redondo Beach) two years prior, in response to the recall of Senator [[Josh Newman (politician)|Josh Newman]], would allow a targeted incumbent to be a candidate on the recall ballot;{{cite web|url=https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/03/recall-rules-gavin-newsom-trouble/|website=CalMatters|title=How California's recall rules could spell trouble for Gavin Newsom|first=Ben|last=Christopher|date=March 8, 2021}} the second, authored by Senator Josh Newman (who by 2020 had reclaimed his lost state senate seat) would have allowed targets of recall campaigns to access the lists of recall petition signers and try to persuade them to remove their signatures. Neither bill would have impacted the 2021 recall election.{{cite web|url=https://calmatters.org/commentary/2021/04/california-newsom-recall-legislation-signatures/|title=Bills would hamstring future California recalls|first=Dan|last=Walters|date=April 14, 2021|website=CalMatters}} Newman's proposed law (Senate Bill 663) cleared the State Senate's Elections Committee on April 12, but he pulled the bill before it headed to the Judiciary Committee{{cite news|title=California bill that would let recall targets see who signed petition clears Senate committee|url=https://ktla.com/news/california/california-bill-that-would-let-recall-targets-see-who-signed-petition-to-oust-them-clears-senate-committee/|date=April 12, 2021|website=[[KTLA]]|agency=[[Associated Press]]}}{{Dead link|date=September 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}{{cite news|title=Bill to reveal names of recall signers won't move ahead|url=https://apnews.com/article/government-and-politics-9084bbdac922f93117326e707931d914|date=April 20, 2021|work=Associated Press| first=Kathleen| last=Ronayne}} after it received fierce opposition from proponents of the 2021 recall over privacy and voter intimidation concerns.{{cite Oppose Bill To Let Future Recall Targets Access Signature Lists|first=Nicole|last=Nixon|date=April 12, 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://ktla.com/news/california/california-bill-seeking-to-reveal-names-of-recall-petition-signers-wont-move-ahead/|title=California bill seeking to reveal names of recall petition signers July 2021, Senator Allen's bill (Senate Constitutional Amendment 3) was on hold in the legislative "suspense file".{{cite web|url=https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB660|title=Bill History|website=California Legislative Information}} In September 2021, while voting in the recall election was underway, Democratic State Assembly Speaker [[Anthony Rendon (politician)|Anthony Rendon]] said discussions were being held to alter California's recall process; support and opposition to changes in the recall process in California have fallen along partisan lines.{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/14/us/california-recall-constitutional-amendment.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20211228/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/14/us/california-recall-constitutional-amendment.html |archive-date=2021-12-28 |url-access=limited |title=As California Votes, It Rethinks Its Tradition of Direct Democracy – The New York Times |work=[[The New York Times]] |date= |access-date=September 15, 2021}}{{cbignore}} Any major changes to the recall process must be approved by California's voters via an amendment to the [[Constitution of California]].{{Cite web|url=https://timesofsandiego.com/politics/2021/09/19/california-democrats-begin-push-to-change-states-recall-election-rules/|title=California Democrats Begin Push to Change State's Recall Election Rules|date=September 20, 2021|website=Times of San Diego}} == Fundraising == California's recall process requires that campaigns supporting challengers adhere to the usual campaign finance limits for political candidates, while there is no dollar limit for a donor's contribution to the campaign of the defending incumbent, nor for donations to groups advocating narrowly for the recall of the incumbent while not supporting any specific challenger.{{cite web|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article250047379.html|title=Gavin Newsom can raise unlimited money in a recall. Candidates to replace him can't|website=[[The Sacramento Bee]]|first=Sophia|last=Bollag}} For the 2021 recall election, the maximum amount that a donor could have given to a candidate (other than Newsom) was $32,400.{{cite web|url=https://www.sfgate.com/gavin-newsom-recall/article/Larry-Ellison-apparently-big-fan-Caitlyn-Jenner-16284920.php|title=Larry Ellison is apparently a real big fan of Caitlyn Jenner|date=June 30, 2021|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle|SFGate]]|first=Joshua|last=Bote}} By June 2021, the three biggest donors to Newsom's campaign against the recall were the California Association of Realtors, the [[California Democratic Party]], and [[Reed Hastings]].{{cite web |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2021/newsom-california-recall-donors/ |title=Biggest donors funding the California recall campaign of Gov. Newsom |website=[[San Francisco Chronicle]] |last1=Gardiner |first1=Dustin |last2=Sumida |first2=Nami |date=June 29, 2021 |access-date=July 2, 2021}} Prominent donors against the recall also included [[Steven Spielberg]], [[George Soros]], [[Jeffrey Katzenberg]], [[Peter Chernin]], [[J.J. Abrams]] and Katie McGrath, [[Laurene Powell Jobs]], and [[Marissa Mayer]].{{cite web|url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/Hollywood-celebrity-donors-pile-into-California-16271901.php|title=Hollywood celebrity donors pile into California governor Newsom recall election|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]|last=Gardiner|first=Dustin|date=June 25, 2021|access-date=July 2, 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/07/06/former-yahoo-ceo-marissa-mayer-gives-newsom-200k-to-defeat-recall-1388047|title=Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer gives Newsom $200K to defeat recall|first=Jeremy B.|last=White|website=[[Politico]]|date=July 6, 2021}} By June 3, 2021, labor unions across the state donated $2 million to Newsom's campaign against the recall and union leaders, while saying their side was already favored by voters, promised a get-out-the-vote drive to "make sure we secure those votes and talk to our members to ensure that base" through a door-to-door canvassing effort.{{cite web|url=https://politi.co/3vTjHgA|title=Newsom counting on labor union army to tank the California recall|first=Jeremy B.|last=White|website=[[Politico|Politico Pro]]|date=June 3, 2021}} While organizers of the recall campaign said the effort was driven by grassroots supporters angry over pandemic restrictions and Newsom's attendance at the French Laundry dinner that defied his own guidelines, over half of the $4 million raised by recall proponents by March 2021 originated from two dozen Republican groups, along with wealthy companies and individuals, including [[Douglas Leone]], [[David O. Sacks]] and [[Chamath Palihapitiya]].{{cite news |last1=Gardiner |first1=Dustin |title=Recall bankrolled by mega-donors, national Republicans — and retirees |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/politics/newsom-recall-bankrolled-by-wealthy-mega-donors-national-republicans-and-retirees/ar-BB1ecewi |agency=[[San Francisco Chronicle]] |date=March 3, 2021}} Recall proponents said there was greater voter energy in favor of the recall and that despite having a small budget, an "unparalleled" volunteer base collected more than enough signatures for the "purposeful and organic" recall effort. By May 26, 2021, $11.1 million and $4.6 million went to the pro-Newsom and pro-recall sides, respectively, with most funding for both sides originating from the same wealthy enclaves around the state.{{cite web|url=https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-recall-campaigns-funding/|title=Who's funding the Newsom recall campaigns?|date=May 26, 2021|website=CalMatters|first=Ben|last=Christopher}} On August 4, 2021, the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' published updated campaign finance data for the upcoming recall election: Newsom's campaign was by far in the lead with $51 million raised, while $5.8 million had been raised by pro-recall committees unaffiliated with a candidate (most of the $5.8 million raised had already been spent during the signature gathering phase). Among challengers who had raised over a million dollars, [[John H. Cox|John Cox]] reported the most, with $7.6 million (largely self-funded), followed by Faulconer, who reported $3.4 million (raised over a six-month period), and Elder, who reported over $1 million (raised over a three-week period).{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-04/recall-fundraising-newsom-jenner-elder-cox-fundraising|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|title=Newsom and his allies raise tens of millions more than recall backers and GOP candidates|last1=Mehta|first1=Seema|last2=Moore|first2=Maloy|date=August 4, 2021}} After surviving the recall election, Newsom would decide the fate of numerous bills passed in the legislature and determine policy that could affect donors to his anti-recall campaign, which included the film and tech industries, real estate and labor union interests, and Native American tribes, who had collectively donated tens of millions of dollars to fight the recall (being unencumbered by donation limits), in what was described as a unique opportunity to attempt to buy influence in California's government.{{Cite web|url=https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/10/newsom-recall-big-donors/|title=What's at stake for Newsom's biggest recall campaign donors|first=Laurel|last=Rosenhall|date=October 4, 2021|via=calmatters.org}} ==Campaign== === Qualified replacement candidates === To have been listed on the ballot as a replacement candidate, a candidate must have been a [[Citizenship of the United States|United States citizen]] and registered to vote in California, submitted signatures from 65 registered voters and paid a $4,194.94 filing fee (which could be waived with the submission of 7,000 signatures of registered voters). Candidates who had been convicted of a felony involving bribery or embezzlement of public money were not allowed to run. The deadline for filing was July 16, 2021. Forty-six candidates qualified to appear on the recall ballot, consisting of 24 Republicans, nine Democrats, two Greens, one Libertarian, and ten no party preference. Four of the 46 candidates qualified after a Sacramento County judge invalidated application of [[California Senate Bill 27 (2019)|SB 27]] on recall elections and ordered California's Secretary of State to add candidates who did not meet requirements for tax return disclosure. The list of candidates on the ballot was certified on July 21, 2021.{{cite web |title=Recall Notice to Candidates |url=https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/notice-to-candidates.pdf |publisher=California Secretary of State |access-date=July 18, 2021 |date=July 17, 2021 |archive-date=July 18, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210718055328/https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/notice-to-candidates.pdf }}{{cite web|url=https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/2021-ca-gov-recall|website=[[California Secretary of State]]|title=California Gubernatorial Recall Election – September 14, 2021|access-date=July 20, 2021|archive-date=July 20, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210720102347/https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/2021-ca-gov-recall}}{{cite web|url=https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/07/newsom-recall-larry-elder/|title=Judge puts Larry Elder on recall ballot, throws out tax return requirement|first=Laurel|last=Rosenhall|date=July 21, 2021|website=CalMatters}} Additionally, seven [[write-in]] candidates were certified by the secretary of state on September 3.{{cite web|url=https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/certified-list-writein.pdf|title=CERTIFIED LIST OF WRITE-IN CANDIDATES SEPTEMBER 14, 2021, CALIFORNIA GUBERNATORIAL RECALL ELECTION|website=[[California Secretary of State]]|date=September 3, 2021|access-date= September 4, 2021}} Of the write-in candidates, their party affiliation consisted of two Democrats, one Republican, one American Independent, and three no party preference. [[Green Party of the United States|Green]] candidate in the [[2003 California gubernatorial recall election]] |[[Vista, California|Vista]] |} === Debates === The [[Richard Nixon Foundation]] announced plans for two debates during the month of August 2021: the first on August 4, and the second on August 22. The first debate was a 90-minute televised event held at the [[Nixon Presidential Library]] in [[Yorba Linda]], California. Six Republican candidates (Faulconer, Elder, Cox, Jenner, Kiley, and Ose) were invited to participate, along with Newsom. The Nixon Foundation announced that all the Republican candidates, with the exception of Jenner, had accepted the invitation, and Gov. Newsom had not responded. A day after the debate was announced with Elder as a participant, the Elder campaign issued a statement that he would not attend the debate.{{cite news|first= Chris|last= Jennewein|title=Larry Elder Won't Debate Other Calif. Republicans in 'Circular Firing Squad'| date=July 24, 2021|url=https://timesofsandiego.com/politics/2021/07/24/larry-elder-wont-debate-other-calif-republicans-in-circular-firing-squad/|website=[[Times of San Diego]]}}{{cite web|website=[[Newsweek]]|url=https://www.newsweek.com/larry-elder-attend-fundraiser-instead-first-gop-california-recall-debate-1613141|first=Meghan|last=Roos|date=July 26, 2021|title=Larry Elder to Attend Fundraiser Instead of First GOP California Recall Debate}}{{Cite news| url=https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/local/california-recall-election-candidates-debate-nixon-presidential-library-gavin-newsom/2646350/|title=Here Are the Five California Recall Election Candidates Who Will Debate Aug. 4 at Richard Nixon Presidential Library| first =Jonathan| last= Lloyd| date=July 23, 2021|website=[[KNBC]]}} During the August 17 debate in Sacramento, Cox was served with a [[subpoena]] while on stage, and on camera. The subpoena by a San Diego County court was for failure to pay a debt of about $100,000 from his [[2018 California gubernatorial election|2018 gubernatorial campaign]]. Ose had initially accepted the invitation to appear at the same debate, but dropped out of the race the day of the debate, and therefore did not attend.{{cite news|title=California GOP recall candidate served with subpoena during debate|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/08/18/politics/california-recall-candidate-john-cox-subpoena/index.html|first1= Alexandra| last1= Meeks| first2 = Veronica| last2= Stracqualursi| publisher =CNN| date= August 18, 2021}} Elder announced that he would not attend the debate, nor any other debate that Newsom was not attending.{{cite news|title=Republican rivals attack recall frontrunner Elder in California debate| url=https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/08/17/republican-rivals-attack-recall-frontrunner-larry-elder-in-california-debate-1390165|date=August 17, 2020|publisher=[[Politico]]|first=Jeremy B.|last=White}} During the August 25 debate in Sacramento, [[Kevin Paffrath]] called on the other three candidates onstage (Faulconer, Cox, and Kiley) to drop out of the race and endorse him, stating he feared a [[Lame duck (politics)|lame-duck]] governor would get nothing done.{{cite web |title=Recap: KCRA 3 and San Francisco Chronicle gubernatorial recall debate |url=https://www.kcra.com/article/california-gubernatorial-recall-debate-aug-25-watch-live-kcra-san-francisco-chronicle/37388891#|first=Hilda|last=Flores|website=kcra.com|date=August 26, 2021}} {| class="wikitable" |-† ! style="background-color:#DEDEBD" | '''−0.15%''' |} {{collapse bottom}} ==Aftermath== ===Turnout and participation=== The number of valid votes cast on the recall question (question 1) was vastly greater than the number cast on the replacement question (question 2). The Newsom campaign's official message to voters had been to vote "no" on the recall and to ignore the replacement question.{{cite web |last1=Christopher |first1=Ben |title='Nobody' Beat GOP Frontrunner Larry Elder by Wide Margin in California Recall |url=https://timesofsandiego.com/politics/2021/09/18/nobody-beat-gops-larry-elder-by-wide-margin-in-california-recall-election/ |website=Times of San Diego |access-date=September 19, 2021 |date=September 18, 2021}}{{cite web |last1=Gardiner |first1=Dustin |title=Larry Elder leads replacement field, but nearly half of recall voters skipped second question |url=https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/Larry-Elder-leads-replacement-field-but-nearly-16460015.php |website=San Francisco Chronicle |access-date=September 19, 2021 |date=September 15, 2021}} In the end, the No vote was similar to Newsom's vote share in 2018, and only [[Merced County, California|Merced County]] voted Yes after backing Newsom in that election. === Commentary after election === In an October 2021 interview with [[Chuck Todd]] at the [[Milken Institute]] Global Conference, Newsom commented on the personal impact of the recall, saying "it's hard", and that it was the result of "personal stupidity", which "took a life of its own" and was "weaponized" by opponents, and, "I mean, we colored it in. I took responsibility."{{cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/meet-the-press/gavin-newsom-reflects-recall-discusses-upcoming-challenges-n1282144|title=Gavin Newsom reflects on the recall, discusses upcoming challenges|website=NBC News|date=22 October 2021|first1=Chuck|last1=Todd|first2=Mark|last2=Murray|first3=Ben|last3=Kamisar|first4=Benjy |last4=Sarlin}} Recall candidate [[Larry Elder]]'s support for the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]], being unpopular among California's electorate, as well as his status as a front-runner and likely gubernatorial replacement if the recall was successful, were reported to have helped Newsom defeat it. Mid-summer polling conducted two months prior to election day suggested a close race. Newsom ultimately defeated the recall with a margin of roughly 24 percent after mobilizing Democrats to vote with a message that framed the race as a referendum on him versus Elder and their pandemic policy proposals. Newsom's campaigning had also invoked Elder's connections to the inner circle of former president [[Donald Trump]],{{cite web|url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article253647713.html|title=Larry Elder is leader among California recall candidates. That might help Gavin Newsom|website=The Sacramento Bee|date=August 23, 2021|last1=Bollag|first1=Sophia}}{{cite web|last=Reston |first=Maeve |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/09/14/politics/larry-elder-covid-newsom-recall/index.html |title=How Larry Elder has helped Gavin Newsom in California's recall election – CNNPolitics |publisher=Cnn.com |date= September 14, 2021|access-date=September 15, 2021}} as well as his history of provocative right-wing rhetoric as a radio talk show host.{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-13/skelton-recall-newsom-elder-poll|title=Column: Larry Elder joining the recall race was the best thing that could've happened to Newsom|date=September 13, 2021|website=Los Angeles Times}} Exit polling suggested the result fell along partisan lines, with 94 percent of self-reported Democrats saying they voted against the recall and 89 percent of self-reported Republicans saying they voted to remove Newsom from office.{{Cite news|last=Rosenhall|first=Laurel|date=September 16, 2021|title=A partisan recall puts California Republican Party in disarray|work=CalMatters|url=http://calmatters.org/politics/2021/09/california-recall-republican-party-disarray/|access-date=October 28, 2021}} The recall was widely invoked following the victory of Republican [[Glenn Youngkin]] two months later in the [[2021 Virginia gubernatorial election]] (where Democrat Joe Biden had [[2020 United States presidential election in Virginia|won in 2020]] by 10 points); Virginia's race featured similar campaigning on education, the pandemic, and former president Trump.{{cite
