Incumbent Governor [[Phil Murphy]] was first elected in [[2017 New Jersey gubernatorial election|2017]] with 56% of the vote{{cite web |url=https://www.cnn.com/election/2017/results/new-jersey-governor/ |title=New Jersey Governor race results 2017 |website=[[CNN]] |publisher=[[WarnerMedia]] |date=November 7, 2017}} and won re-election to a second term. Murphy and his running mate, Lt. Gov. [[Sheila Oliver]], defeated the Republican ticket of [[Jack Ciattarelli]] and [[Diane Allen]], 51.2% to 48%. Murphy formally announced his intention to run for a second term on October 1, 2020.{{cite web |first=David |last=Wildstein |url=https://newjerseyglobe.com/governor/murphy-formally-launches-bid-for-2nd-term-as-governor-will-run-with-oliver/ |title=Murphy formally launches bid for 2nd term as governor, will run with Oliver |website=[[New Jersey Globe]] |publisher=Sea of Reeds Media |date=October 1, 2020 |access-date=November 9, 2020}} Primaries were held on June 8, 2021. Murphy, who won the Democratic nomination unopposed after his two primary challengers were disqualified, faced Ciattarelli, [[Green Party of the United States|Green]] nominee Madelyn Hoffman, [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] nominee Gregg Mele, and [[Socialist Workers Party (United States)|Socialist Workers Party]] nominee Joanne Kuniansky in the general election. The race was considered by many media outlets to be a "safe" or "likely" Democratic hold, as Murphy had led a majority of pre-election polls by double digits.{{cite web|url = https://www.realclearpolitics.com/epolls/2021/governor/nj/new_jersey_governor_ciattarelli_vs_murphy-7372.html|title = New Jersey Governor|work = [[RealClearPolitics]]|accessdate = November 4, 2021}} However, Murphy defeated Ciattarelli by a much smaller margin than expected. Murphy is the first Democratic governor of New Jersey to win re-election since [[Brendan Byrne]] in [[1977 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1977]], as well as the first candidate of the same party as the incumbent [[President of the United States|U.S. president]] to win since [[Thomas Kean]] in [[1985 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1985]]. This is also the first New Jersey gubernatorial election since [[2009 New Jersey gubernatorial election|2009]] where both the Democratic and Republican nominees received more than one million votes each.{{cite web|title=Murphy wins bruising N.J. governor's race, narrowly beating Ciattarelli for 2nd term|date=November 3, 2021|url=https://www.nj.com/politics/2021/11/murphy-wins-bruising-nj-governors-race-narrowly-beating-ciattarelli-for-2nd-term.html}} It also was the first New Jersey gubernatorial election where the Green Party candidate placed third. Murphy also became the first Democrat to win a New Jersey gubernatorial election without carrying [[Gloucester County, New Jersey|Gloucester]] and [[Cumberland County, New Jersey|Cumberland]] Counties since [[Robert B. Meyner]] in [[1953 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1953]], and the first Democrat to win a gubernatorial election without carrying [[Atlantic County, New Jersey|Atlantic County]] since [[Richard J. Hughes]] in [[1961 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1961]]. Atlantic County voted for the losing candidate for the first time since [[1993 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1993]]. Also, this was the first New Jersey gubernatorial election in which [[Somerset County, New Jersey|Somerset County]] voted more Democratic than the state as a whole since [[1910 New Jersey gubernatorial election|1910]]. Murphy became the first New Jersey Governor since Brendan Byrne to win both of his elections with a majority of the vote each time. It was the first single-digit Democratic win in a governor's election since 1961. Murphy received the most votes for a Democrat or any governor since 1989, and Ciattarelli received the most for a Republican since 2013.{{cite web|url=https://abc7ny.com/nj-election-results-live-phil-murphy-jack-ciattarelli-who-is-winning-governor-race-new-jersey/11193247/|title=LIVE NJ Election 2021 Updates: Phil Murphy wins reelection for governor in NJ over Jack Ciattarell|work=[[WABC-TV]]|date=November 3, 2021|access-date=November 3, 2021|archive-date=November 3, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211103232028/https://abc7ny.com/nj-election-results-live-phil-murphy-jack-ciattarelli-who-is-winning-governor-race-new-jersey/11193247/|url-status=dead}}{{Cite web|title=New Jersey Governor Election Results 2021 {{!}} Live Map Updates {{!}} Voting by County|url=https://www.politico.com/election-results/2021/new-jersey/governor/|access-date=2021-11-03|website=Politico|language=en}} Despite failing to flip the state, Ciattarelli swung the state more Republican from the [[2020 United States presidential election in New Jersey|2020 presidential election]] than [[Glenn Youngkin]], the Republican candidate for [[2021 Virginia gubernatorial election|the concurrent Virginia gubernatorial election]], did in his respective state even as he managed to flip the governorship. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Virginia|Governor]] | before_election = [[Ralph Northam]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Glenn Youngkin]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 54.9% {{increase}} 7.7 [[percentage point|pp]]{{Cite report|title=SUMMARY OF VIRGINIA REGISTRATION & TURNOUT STATISTICS|language=en|publisher=Virginia Department of Elections|url=https://www.elections.virginia.gov/resultsreports/registrationturnout-statistics|access-date=2023-03-22}} }}{{Elections in Virginia sidebar}} The '''2021 Virginia gubernatorial election''' was held on November 2, 2021, to elect the [[governor of Virginia]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] businessman [[Glenn Youngkin]] defeated [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former governor [[Terry McAuliffe]]. Youngkin succeeded Democratic incumbent [[Ralph Northam]] who was [[Term limits in the United States|term-limited]] and ineligible to seek a second consecutive term. The Democratic Party held its [[primary elections]] on June 8, 2021. McAuliffe won the primary with 62% of the vote.{{Cite web |last=Kilgore |first=Ed |date=2020-12-14 |title=Is Terry McAuliffe the Best Virginia Democrats Can Offer for Governor? |url=https://nymag.com/intelligencer/2020/12/democrat-terry-mcauliffe-governor-virginia.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201216215358/https://nymag.com/intelligencer/2020/12/democrat-terry-mcauliffe-governor-virginia.html |archive-date=December 16, 2020 |access-date=2021-01-02 |website=[[Intelligencer (website)|Intelligencer]] |language=en}}{{cite web |date=June 8, 2021 |title=Virginia Primary Election Results |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/06/08/us/elections/results-virginia-primary-elections.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210608232333/https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/06/08/us/elections/results-virginia-primary-elections.html |archive-date=June 8, 2021 |access-date=June 8, 2021 |website=[[The New York Times]]}} The Republican Party held its convention on May 8, 2021, in which Youngkin won the nomination on May 10.{{cite web |last1=Wilson |first1=Patrick |date=March 12, 2021 |title=After months of fighting, Va. Republicans appear to have finalized nomination process |url=https://richmond.com/news/state-and-regional/after-months-of-fighting-va-republicans-appear-to-have-finalized-nomination-process/article_cbccd897-d89f-5cb2-ad50-411610723e43.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210313175321/https://richmond.com/news/state-and-regional/after-months-of-fighting-va-republicans-appear-to-have-finalized-nomination-process/article_cbccd897-d89f-5cb2-ad50-411610723e43.html |archive-date=March 13, 2021 |access-date=March 12, 2021 |website=[[Richmond Times-Dispatch]]}}{{cite news |last=Gabriel |first=Trip |date=2021-05-11 |title=Glenn Youngkin Wins G.O.P. Nomination for Virginia Governor |language=en |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/05/10/us/politics/glenn-youngkin-virginia-governor-republicans.html |url-status=live |access-date=2021-05-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210511162029/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/05/10/us/politics/glenn-youngkin-virginia-governor-republicans.html |archive-date=May 11, 2021 |issn=0362-4331}} At the start of the general election, McAuliffe was widely considered to be the favorite,{{Cite web |title=Roanoke College Poll: McAuliffe leads Youngkin in race for Virginia Governor |url=https://www.roanoke.edu/news/rc_poll_politics_aug_2021 |access-date=2026-02-05 |website=www.roanoke.edu |language=en}} but Youngkin closed the gap throughout most of the fall, leading most analysts to label the election as a toss-up. Youngkin ended up narrowly defeating McAuliffe by 63,688 votes. Youngkin's coattails seemingly benefitted fellow down-ballot candidates [[Winsome Earle-Sears]] and [[Jason Miyares]] who concurrently won elections for [[2021 Virginia lieutenant gubernatorial election|Lieutenant Governor]] and [[2021 Virginia Attorney General election|Attorney General]]; 2021 remains the only time the Republican Party has won statewide elections in Virginia since [[2009 Virginia gubernatorial election|2009]]. The economy, education, public health, and cultural issues were centerpieces of Youngkin's campaign.{{Cite web|author=Ariel Edwards-Levy|title=Independent voters favor Youngkin as he clinches victory in Virginia, CNN exit poll shows|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/11/02/politics/virginia-exit-polls/index.html|access-date=2021-11-03|website=[[CNN]]|date=November 2, 2021 }}{{cite web|last=Prokop|first=Andrew|date=2021-11-03|title=What Glenn Youngkin's Virginia win means for Democrats|url=https://www.vox.com/2021/11/3/22752593/virginia-governor-results-youngkin-wins|access-date=2021-11-03|website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|language=en}}{{Cite web|last=Graham|first=David A.|date=2021-11-02|title=Tonight Is a Test of What Trumpism Could Be Without Trump|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2021/11/glenn-youngkin-virginia-election-2021/620561/|access-date=2021-11-03|website=[[The Atlantic]]|language=en}} Youngkin promised to ban the teaching of [[critical race theory]] within [[Public school (government-funded)|public school]]s on "day one", push back against certain COVID-19 restrictions including [[COVID-19 vaccination mandates in the United States|vaccination mandates]] and mask mandates, and advocate for [[small government]] within the state of Virginia.{{Cite web|title=In Virginia, Republicans see education, curriculum fears as a path to victory|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/virginia-republicans-see-education-curriculum-fears-path-victory-n1281676|access-date=2021-11-03|website=[[NBC News]]|date=October 17, 2021 |language=en}}{{Cite web|date=2021-10-24|title=Glenn Youngkin targets education in Virginia Gov. race, says he'd ban CRT|url=https://www.newsweek.com/glenn-youngkin-vows-ban-critical-race-theory-1641987|access-date=2021-11-03|website=[[Newsweek]]|language=en}}{{Cite web|last=Barrabi|first=Thomas|date=2021-11-02|title=Virginia governor-elect Youngkin's economic plan includes lower taxes, less regulation|url=https://www.foxbusiness.com/politics/virginia-governor-race-mcauliffe-youngkin-economy|access-date=2021-11-03|website=FOXBusiness|language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Fiske |first=Warren |title=Youngkin offers little proof critical race theory is in 'all' Virginia schools |url=https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2021/aug/10/glenn-youngkin/youngkin-offers-little-proof-critical-race-theory-/ |access-date=2025-07-19 |website=@politifact |language=en-US}} Democrats tried to portray Youngkin as a political ally of [[Donald Trump]], who [[2020 United States presidential election in Virginia|lost Virginia in 2020]], and Trump did indeed express support for Youngkin. Walking a fine line between welcoming the endorsement and demonstrating independence, Youngkin was successfully able to appeal to both Republicans and independents.{{cite news |url=https://www.voachinese.com/a/virginia-election-republican-win-implication-for-biden-20211103/6298368.html |title=Republican political amateur wins Virginia governor election, President Biden's political and governance prospects are worrisome|publisher=VOA |date=2021-11-03 |access-date=2021-11-04 |archive-date=2021-11-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211123163222/https://www.voachinese.com/a/virginia-election-republican-win-implication-for-biden-20211103/6298368.html |url-status=live }} Political analysts believe that the main reason for the Democratic Party's defeat in Virginia was that voters were not satisfied with the performance of President [[Joe Biden]], with whom McAuliffe allied himself.{{cite news |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/564443-biden-hits-trail-for-mcauliffe-in-test-of-his-political-brand/ |title=Biden hits trail for McAuliffe in test of his political brand |work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |first1=Julia |last1=Manchester |first2=Brett |last2=Samuels |date=July 23, 2021 |access-date=January 26, 2023}}Sargent, Greg (November 3, 2021). Later in the debate, Carter called McAuliffe out for mentioning Youngkin and Trump so often. "The debate that we're supposed to be having on this stage is a debate about the future of this commonwealth," he said. "It's about what we stand for and what we're going to fight for. And this is the first opportunity for the Democratic Party to define what it is going to be after Donald Trump is gone. And he is gone. So, we can't just be a party that is opposed to the other guys. We have to fight for something." news|first=Laura|last=Vozzella|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/virginia-politics/virginia-gop-governor-vote-counting/2021/04/21/fbb6760c-a2d6-11eb-a774-7b47ceb36ee8_story.html|title=Three nominating method with May convention looming|url=https://www.wric.com/news/politics/capitol-connection/virginia-gop-settles-on-nominating-method-with-may-convention-looming/|date=April 22, On December 5, 2020, the state Republican Party voted to hold a convention instead of a primary by a vote of 39 to 35.{{Cite web|title=RPV State Central Committee Meeting;Voted Convention for 2021;Live Updates – Bearing Drift|url=https://bearingdrift.com/2020/12/05/rpv-state-central-committee-meeting-voted-convention-for-2021/|access-date=2020-12-05|website=bearingdrift.com|date=December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210322143948/https://bearingdrift.com/2020/12/05/rpv-state-central-committee-meeting-voted-convention-for-2021/|url-status=dead}} State Senator [[Amanda Chase]] initially indicated that she would run as an independent,{{Cite web|last1=Oliver|first1=Ned|date=2020-12-05|title=Chase promises to run as independent for governor after Va. GOP opts for convention over primary|url=https://www.virginiamercury.com/2020/12/05/chase-threatens-to-run-as-independent-for-governor-as-va-gop-opts-for-convention-over-primary/|access-date=2020-12-05|website=Virginia Mercury|language=en|archive-date=March 22, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210322144013/https://www.virginiamercury.com/2020/12/05/chase-threatens-to-run-as-independent-for-governor-as-va-gop-opts-for-convention-over-primary/|url-status=live}} but she later decided to seek nomination at the convention; on the day of the convention, she acknowledged that if she did not win the nomination, she may reconsider and run as an independent, although she eventually decided against this.{{cite tweet |last=Chase |first=Amanda |author-link=Amanda Chase |user=AmandaChaseVA |number=1391150084377677826 |date=May 8, 2021 |title=If RPV steals this election for Pete I still have plenty of time to run as an independent. Clear corruption by RPV, I will not honor a pledge if the Party cannot run a fair process. |language=en |access-date=June 12, 2021 }} Faced with pressure from the Chase campaign and activists to return to a primary, the state committee debated scrapping the convention on January 23, 2021. These efforts were unsuccessful and the party reaffirmed their decision to hold a convention.{{cite news |last1=Oliver |first1=Ned |title=Virginia Republicans stick with nominating convention |url=https://www.virginiamercury.com/2021/01/24/virginia-republicans-stick-with-convention-as-messy-fight-continues/ |access-date=January 25, 2021 |work=Virginia Mercury |date=January 24, 2021 |archive-date=March 22, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210322144016/https://www.virginiamercury.com/2021/01/24/virginia-republicans-stick-with-convention-as-messy-fight-continues/ |url-status=live}} On February 9, 2021, the Chase campaign sued the Republican Party of Virginia, arguing that the convention is illegal under [[COVID-19]]-related executive orders signed by Governor [[Ralph Northam]].{{Cite web|last1=Manchester|first1=Julia|date=February 9, 2021|title=Republican gubernatorial candidate sues Virginia GOP over nominating process|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/538075-republican-state-senator-sues-virginia-gop-over-nominating-process|url-status=live|access-date=February 9, 2021|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|archive-date=March 22, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210322144003/https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/538075-republican-state-senator-sues-virginia-gop-over-nominating-process}} The Richmond Circuit Court dismissed the Chase campaign's lawsuit on February 19, 2021.{{Cite web|last1=Manzanares|first1=Keyris|date=February 19, 2021|title=Judge blocks Sen. Amanda Chase's lawsuit challenging Virginia GOP nomination plans|url=https://www.wric.com/news/politics/capitol-connection/judge-blocks-sen-amanda-chases-lawsuit-challenging-virginia-gop-nomination-plansw|access-date=February 19, 2021|website=[[WRIC-TV|WRIC]]}} {{Dead link|date=November 2021 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes}} The Republican Party of Virginia announced on March 26, 2021, that seven gubernatorial candidates had qualified to appear on the convention ballot.{{Cite web|date=2021-03-26|title=RPV Announces Qualified Convention Candidates|url=https://virginia.gop/rpv-announces-qualified-convention-candidates/|access-date=2021-03-26|website=Republican Party of Virginia|language=en|archive-date=March 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210326211229/https://virginia.gop/rpv-announces-qualified-convention-candidates/|url-status=live}} On April 11, 2021, the state Republican Party Rules Committee voted to tabulate the ballots by hand; three days later, however, the committee reversed itself and decided to use a vendor's software-based tabulation method. On April 20, 2021, five candidates (Amanda Chase, Kirk Cox, Sergio de la Peña, Peter Doran, and Glenn Youngkin) participated in a forum at [[Liberty University]] in [[Lynchburg, Virginia|Lynchburg]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.wric.com/news/politics/capitol-connection/5-republicans-in-virginia-governors-race-make-their-pitch-to-voters-during-liberty-university-forum/|title=Key takeaways from the Republican gubernatorial forum in Lynchburg|date=2021-04-20|access-date=2021-04-22|last=Mirshahi|first=Dean|work=WRIC ABC 8News |archive-date=April 22, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422123703/https://www.wric.com/news/politics/capitol-connection/5-republicans-in-virginia-governors-race-make-their-pitch-to-voters-during-liberty-university-forum/|url-status=live}} Two candidates, Octavia Johnson and Pete Snyder, did not attend the forum.{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/virginia-politics/republicans-running-for-virginia-governor-appear-at-liberty-university-forum/2021/04/20/b94d408e-a1eb-11eb-a7ee-949c574a09ac_story.html|title=Republicans running for Virginia governor appear at Liberty University forum|date=2021-04-20|access-date=2021-04-22|last=Vozzella|first=Laura|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|archive-date=October 28, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028122134/https://gum.criteo.com/syncframe?origin=publishertag&topUrl=www.washingtonpost.com|url-status=live}} The state Republican convention to select the party's nominees for governor, lieutenant governor, and attorney general took place on May 8, 2021, in "unassembled" format, with ballots to be cast remotely at up to 37 locations statewide using [[instant-runoff voting|ranked-choice voting]]. The complex process fueled internal party disputes.{{cite news|first=Laura|last=Vozzella|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/virginia-politics/virginia-gop-convention/2021/04/04/4bfe8fc4-9228-11eb-a74e-1f4cf89fd948_story.html|title=Unorthodox Republican contest for Virginia governor breeds confusion, suspicion|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=April 4, 2021|access-date=October 27, 2021|archive-date=April 9, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210409124342/https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/virginia-politics/virginia-gop-convention/2021/04/04/4bfe8fc4-9228-11eb-a74e-1f4cf89fd948_story.html|url-status=live}} Up to 40,000 people were anticipated to become delegates, although not all would necessarily cast votes. Local Republican Party leaders control the application process to become a delegate, decide who can participate (voter registration in Virginia does not include a space to indicate party affiliation), and select the convention voting site. In the preceding Virginia Republican gubernatorial convention, 12,000 participated. [[Orthodox Jewish]] Virginia Republicans asked the party to allow absentee voting for religious reasons (May 8 is on the [[Jewish Sabbath]]), but the State Central Committee initially voted down the request, failing to achieve the 75% supermajority needed to change the rules.{{cite news|first=Laura|last=Vozzella|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/virginia-politics/virginia-republican-convention-orthodox-jews/2021/04/23/3169c904-a442-11eb-85fc-06664ff4489d_story.html|title=Virginia GOP won't let Orthodox Jews vote absentee in Sabbath-day convention|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=April 23, 2021|access-date=April 25, 2021|archive-date=April 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210425164505/https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/virginia-politics/virginia-republican-convention-orthodox-jews/2021/04/23/3169c904-a442-11eb-85fc-06664ff4489d_story.html|url-status=live}} However, the Virginia GOP ultimately reversed course and allowed those with religious objections to vote in the May 8 convention via absentee ballots. Republican candidates Kirk Cox, Peter Doran, and Glenn Youngkin had criticized the previous decision to not accommodate Orthodox Jews.{{Cite web|url=https://www.wric.com/news/politics/capitol-connection/in-reversal-virginia-gop-will-allow-those-with-religious-obligations-to-vote-absentee-in-may-8-convention/|title=In reversal, Virginia GOP will allow those with religious obligations to vote absentee in May 8 convention|work=WRIC ABC 8News |date=April 26, 2021|access-date=April 26, 2021|archive-date=April 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426224446/https://www.wric.com/news/politics/capitol-connection/in-reversal-virginia-gop-will-allow-those-with-religious-obligations-to-vote-absentee-in-may-8-convention/|url-status=live}} Cox received crucial endorsements of [[Bob McDonnell]] and [[George Allen (American politician)|George Allen]], the former of whom was the last statewide elected Republican (alongside [[Bill Bolling]] and [[Ken Cuccinelli]]) in Virginia prior to 2022. He was regarded by some as the establishment favorite heading into the convention.{{Cite web|last=Houck|first=Caroline|date=2021-05-08|title=Virginia Republicans' messy, Trumpy race to pick a nominee for governor|url=https://www.vox.com/22423524/virginia-gop-trump-convention-governor-election|access-date=2022-02-09|website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|language=en}} Nonetheless, he finished fourth on the first voting round behind Glenn Youngkin, Pete Snyder, and Amanda Chase. The suit also alleged the witnesses violated state law by witnessing a signing that did not occur.{{cite news|url=https://apnews.com/article/virginia-election-2020-b0775646f6ca89d5f83106c86de59506|title=Virginia Republicans file suit over McAuliffe's paperwork|date=2021-08-26|access-date=2021-09-16|archive-date=September 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210916153151/https://apnews.com/article/virginia-election-2020-b0775646f6ca89d5f83106c86de59506|url-status=live}} === Debates === ==== Canceled debates ==== On July 12, Glenn Youngkin announced he would not take part in the July 24 debate hosted by the [[Virginia Bar Association]] because of a donation made by one of the moderators, [[Judy Woodruff]].{{Cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/government-and-politics-election-2020-522265ba9fd99fc0e96ce67c68c52cec|title=Youngkin declines debate in part over moderator Woodruff|website=[[Associated Press]]|date=2021-07-12|access-date=2021-08-31|archive-date=August 31, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210831181105/https://apnews.com/article/government-and-politics-election-2020-522265ba9fd99fc0e96ce67c68c52cec|url-status=live}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.wsls.com/news/politics/2021/07/12/glenn-youngkin-not-participating-in-gubernatorial-debate-in-hot-springs-agrees-to-three-others/|title=Glenn Youngkin not participating in gubernatorial debate in Hot Springs, agrees to three others|date=2021-07-12|access-date=2021-08-31|archive-date=August 31, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210831181107/https://www.wsls.com/news/politics/2021/07/12/glenn-youngkin-not-participating-in-gubernatorial-debate-in-hot-springs-agrees-to-three-others/|url-status=live}} Woodruff had made a $250 donation to the [[Clinton Foundation]] relief fund after the [[2010 Haiti earthquake]]. The foundation had been run by [[Hillary Clinton|Hillary]] and [[Bill Clinton]], who were close allies to Terry McAuliffe. ==== First debate ==== Youngkin and McAuliffe met at [[Appalachian School of Law]] in [[Grundy, Virginia]] on September 16, 2021, one day before early voting began.{{cite news|url=https://wset.com/news/local/mcauliffe-vs-youngkin-heres-what-you-missed-thursday-nights-debate-glenn-terry-virginia-governor|title=McAuliffe vs. Youngkin: Here's what you missed from Thursday The debate was hosted by ''[[USA Today]]'' Washington Bureau Chief, [[Susan Page]].{{cite news|url=https://wset.com/news/beyond-the-podium/terry-mcauliffe-glenn-youngkin-face-off-thursday-september-16-2021-grundy-southwest-virginia-gubernatorial-debate|title=McAuliffe, Youngkin face-off 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028122124/https://gum.criteo.com/syncframe?topUrl=wset.com|url-status=live}} The debate started with discussion over a recent [[COVID-19 vaccination#Vaccine mandates|COVID-19 mandate]] President [[Joe Biden]] signed requiring federal workers, employees of large companies, and contractors to be vaccinated.{{cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/biden-covid-19-vaccine-mandates-announcement/|title=Biden announces COVID-19 vaccine mandates that will affect 100 million Americans|date=2021-09-10|access-date=2021-09-17|archive-date=September 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210917140349/https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/biden-covid-19-vaccine-mandates-announcement/|url-status=live}}{{cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/terry-mcauliffe-glenn-youngkin-debate-virginia-gubernatorial-race/|title=Vaccine mandates and abortion bans fuel Virginia's first gubernatorial race debate|date=2021-09-17|access-date=2021-09-17|last=Navarro|first=Aaron|archive-date=September 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210917140347/https://www.cbsnews.com/news/terry-mcauliffe-glenn-youngkin-debate-virginia-gubernatorial-race/|url-status=live}} Youngkin doubted if Biden had the power to authorize the mandate, and supported personal choice for receiving the vaccine. McAuliffe supported the mandate and accused Youngkin of spreading [[COVID-19 misinformation|"anti-vax" rhetoric]]. Youngkin denied the claim. McAuliffe also supported requiring vaccines for students over the age of 12.{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/09/16/politics/mcauliffe-youngkin-virginia-governor-debate/index.html|title=McAuliffe and Youngkin spar over Covid vaccine requirements in first Virginia debate|publisher=[[CNN]]|date=September 17, 2021|access-date=September 23, 2021|last1=Warren|first1=Michael|last2=Merica|first2=Dan|archive-date=September 23, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210923175826/https://www.cnn.com/2021/09/16/politics/mcauliffe-youngkin-virginia-governor-debate/index.html|url-status=live}} McAuliffe had also repeatedly made false statements about [[COVID-19]], often inflating the number of cases.{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2021/10/26/terry-mcauliffe-keeps-inflating-coronavirus-numbers/|title=Terry McAuliffe keeps inflating coronavirus numbers|date=October 26, 2021|last=Kessler|first=Glenn|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|type=fact check|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211026235058/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2021/10/26/terry-mcauliffe-keeps-inflating-coronavirus-numbers/|archive-date=October 26, 2021|url-status=live|access-date=October 26, 2021}} About [[climate change]], Youngkin stated he would use all sources of energy to [[climate change mitigation|address climate change]] without "putting [the] entire energy grid at risk for political purposes." McAuliffe called for [[clean energy]] in the state by 2035, and stressed the idea for the state to be a production hub. The discussion then moved to abortion, specifically the recent [[Texas Heartbeat Act]] signed by Texas governor [[Greg Abbott]] (who endorsed Youngkin).{{cite news|url=https://abcnews.com/Politics/mcauliffe-youngkin-spar-vision-commonwealth-1st-va-gubernatorial/story?id=80057575|title=McAuliffe, Youngkin spar over vision for commonwealth in 1st Va. gubernatorial debate|work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|first=Quinn|last=Scanlan|date=2021-09-17|access-date=2021-09-17|archive-date=September 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210917140349/https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/mcauliffe-youngkin-spar-vision-commonwealth-1st-va-gubernatorial/story?id=80057575|url-status=live}} When asked whether he would sign a similar bill, Youngkin stated that he would not sign the bill, was [[anti-abortion]], and supported exclusions in cases such as rape, incest, and when the life of the mother is endangered. He said he supported a "pain-threshold" bill that would ban most abortions at the point when a fetus can feel pain, which proponents of this type of law define as 20 weeks. Youngkin called McAuliffe "the most extreme pro-abortion candidate in America today". In response, McAuliffe stated he was a "brick wall" on women's rights, would protect a woman's decision over abortion, and supported reducing the number of doctors needed to certify a third-trimester abortion from three to one. After supporting an "Election Integrity Taskforce", Youngkin said he did not believe there had been "significant fraud", and called the issue of fraud "a democracy issue". He stressed that he believes that "Joe Biden's our president", and criticized the [[Withdrawal of the United States troops from Afghanistan (2020–2021)|withdrawal from Afghanistan]]. McAuliffe took note of Donald Trump's endorsement of Youngkin, calling him a "Trump wannabe". Both candidates stated they would concede the election if the other came out on top. The final discussion topic was over the economy. McAuliffe attacked Youngkin on his top economic advisor, [[Stephen Moore (writer)|Stephen Moore]], who advised [[Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign]]. Youngkin defended Virginia's [[right-to-work law]]. ==== Second debate ==== Youngkin and McAuliffe met at the [[Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce]] on September 28, 2021.{{Cite web|url=https://web.cvent.com/event/5e9837a7-3094-4e39-9659-df9d79321875/summary|access-date=2021-09-23|title=Top of the Ticket 2021 Gubernatorial Debate|archive-date=September 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210917213249/https://web.cvent.com/event/5e9837a7-3094-4e39-9659-df9d79321875/summary|url-status=live}} The event was hosted by [[Chuck Todd]], moderator of [[NBC]]'s ''[[Meet the Press]]''. Less than a week before the debate, one of the panelists, [[Michael Fauntroy]], withdrew from the debate after tweets against the [[GOP]] and [[Evangelicalism|Evangelicals]] were found.{{cite news|url=https://www.foxnews.com/media/mcauliffe-youngkin-debate-michael-fauntroy|title=Panelist withdraws from upcoming McAuliffe-Youngkin debate after tweets attacking GOP, evangelicals surface|work=[[Fox News]]|date=2021-09-22|access-date=2021-09-23|last=Wulfsohn|first=Joseph|archive-date=September 23, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210923083247/https://www.foxnews.com/media/mcauliffe-youngkin-debate-michael-fauntroy|url-status=live}} On the topic of COVID-19, Youngkin and McAuliffe reiterated their stances on the vaccines. Youngkin stated he believed in mandates for vaccines for [[measles]], [[mumps]] and [[rubella]], but not for COVID-19, saying that "the data associated with those vaccines is something that we should absolutely understand the difference between this vaccine."{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/09/28/politics/virginia-governor-debate-covid-vaccine-mandate/index.html|title=McAuliffe and Youngkin battle over Covid-19 vaccine mandates in Virginia governor's debate|work=[[CNN]]|first=Eric|last=Bradner|date=2021-09-28|access-date=2021-09-29|archive-date=September 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210929131649/https://www.cnn.com/2021/09/28/politics/virginia-governor-debate-covid-vaccine-mandate/index.html|url-status=live}} Youngkin said people should get vaccinated against COVID-19. During the debate, Youngkin noted that Trump was regularly mentioned by McAuliffe, who again called Youngkin a "Trump wannabe."{{cite news|url=https://www.nbcwashington.com/news/politics/first-read-dmv/debate-takeaways-virginia-candidates-on-attack-from-start/2815808/|title=Virginia Gubernatorial Candidates on Attack From Start in Debate|work=NBC Washington|first=Steve|last=Peoples|date=2021-09-28|access-date=2021-09-29|archive-date=September 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210929131651/https://www.nbcwashington.com/news/politics/first-read-dmv/debate-takeaways-virginia-candidates-on-attack-from-start/2815808/|url-status=live}} When asked, Youngkin stated he would support Trump if he were to become the Republican nominee in [[2024 United States presidential election|2024]]. {{party shading/Democratic}}|{{ushr|Virginia|11|11th}} |32.6% | '''66.6%''' | 0.8% | {{party shading/Democratic}}|[[Gerry Connolly]] |} ==Analysis== Youngkin won the election, 50.6% to 48.6%.{{Cite web|url=https://www.whbnews.com/news/2021/11/08/republicans-sweep-virginia-elections/|title=Republicans Sweep Virginia Elections|first=Dan|last=Stark|website=[[Westhampton Beach High School|Westhampton Beach High School News]]|date=November 8, 2021}} The margin of victory was the narrowest margin in a Virginia gubernatorial election [[1989 Virginia gubernatorial election|since 1989]]. McAuliffe conceded the day after the election and congratulated Youngkin, saying he was "proud" to campaign "for the values we so deeply believe in".{{cite news|last1=Martin|first1=Jonathan|last2=Burns|first2=Alexander|last3=Kaplan|first3=Thomas|date=2021-11-03|title=Terry McAuliffe concedes to Glenn Youngkin, a Republican financier, in the Virginia governor's race.|language=en|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/03/us/elections/mcauliffe-concede-virginia-governor.html|access-date=2021-11-03|issn=0362-4331}}{{cite web|last=Swalec|first=Andrea|title='We Came Up Short': Terry McAuliffe Concedes Virginia Governor's Race|url=https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/politics/we-came-up-short-terry-mcauliffe-concedes-virginia-governors-race/3375172/|access-date=2021-11-03|website=NBC New York|date=November 3, 2021 |language=en}} Republicans also flipped the lieutenant governor and attorney general races that were held concurrently,{{cite news|title=Virginia Election Results|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/11/02/us/elections/results-virginia.html|language=en|date=2021-11-02|access-date=2021-11-04}} as well as took control of the [[2021 Virginia House of Delegates election|Virginia House of Delegates]]. This election, as well as the concurrent elections for [[2021 Virginia lieutenant gubernatorial election|lieutenant governor]] and [[2021 Virginia Attorney General election|attorney general]], marked the first time since the [[1969 Virginia gubernatorial election|1969 gubernatorial election]] that a Republican won Virginia without [[Loudoun County, Virginia|Loudoun County]], and the first time since the [[1960 United States presidential election in Virginia|1960 presidential election]] that a Republican won statewide without [[Prince William County, Virginia|Prince William County]]. This is the first time [[Surry County, Virginia|Surry County]] backed the Republican candidate since [[John Warner]]'s largely uncontested [[2002 United States Senate election in Virginia|re-election in 2002]] and the first time [[Prince Edward County, Virginia|Prince Edward County]] or [[Northampton County, Virginia|Northampton County]] voted Republican since [[2009 Virginia gubernatorial election|2009]]. This is also the first time any Virginia statewide candidate has won without at least one of the three [[Northern Virginia]] counties of Loudoun, Prince William, [[Fairfax County, Virginia|Fairfax]], or the independent cities therein. This was the first gubernatorial election since 1989 in which Democrats failed to flip any counties. Over 3.28 million votes were cast, exceeding the 2017 gubernatorial election total by roughly 625,000 and exceeding all other previous Virginia gubernatorial elections by over a million. Youngkin's victory is attributed to the "Youngkin coalition" of largely [[Trump supporters]] and suburbanites, which contributed to a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] victory in the state.Fox News Voter Analysis. (November 2, 2021). [https://static.foxnews.com/foxnews.com/content/uploads/2021/11/FNVA-Virginia_as-of-10pm-results.pdf FNVA-Virginia_as-of-10pm-results.pdf]. ''Fox News''. ''Politico''. Retrieved November 5, 2021. The appeal to suburban voters, who have shifted away from the Republican Party as Donald Trump increasingly influenced it, was attributed to Youngkin's distancing from Trump and hesitancy to openly embrace him. Youngkin's performance in the suburbs near [[Washington, D.C.]] were stronger than that of Trump's margins in the [[2020 United States presidential election]]. During the final days preceding the general election held on November 2, Youngkin campaigned in the [[Washington metropolitan area]] suburbs of Northern Virginia.Merica, Dan; Bradner, Eric; McKend, Eva (October 29, 2021). [https://www.cnn.com/2021/10/29/politics/mcauliffe-youngkin-closing-weekend-virginia/index.html As early voting nears its end, McAuliffe and Youngkin campaign in decidedly different ways]. ''CNN''. Retrieved November 5, 2021. Previous similar attempts to combine a coalition of Trump supporters and suburban voters, including [[Ed Gillespie]]'s run for governor in [[2017 Virginia gubernatorial election|2017]], were met with failure.Geraghty, Jim (November 2, 2021). [https://www.nationalreview.com/corner/what-happens-if-glenn-youngkin-comes-close/ What Happens If Glenn Youngkin Comes Close?]. ''National Review''. Retrieved November 5, 2021.
